links.outcome: AI-PAL discrimination on local historical hospital data versus published validation results
links.effect: AUROC dropped to 0.67 (95% CI 0.61-0.73) for ALL and 0.71 (0.65-0.76) for AML, below the worst original validation cohort (0.78, 0.80).
links.quote: Evaluation of the unmodified AI-PAL algorithm at UME showed a lower performance compared to the four cohorts from the AI-PAL external validation ( Fig. 3 , Supplementary Table S1 ).

links.outcome: Confident diagnoses before versus after local recalibration of PPV/NPV cutoffs
links.effect: Confident ALL among ALL cases rose from 0% to 12.5%; confident positive diagnoses for acute leukaemia rose from 98 to 160; false confident calls rose only slightly (8.7% to 12.5%).
links.quote: With these adjustments, considerably more ‘confident’ predictions were obtained for the UME cohort ( Table 3 ).

links.outcome: Differences between AI-PAL development cohort and local population in disease mix and lab distributions
links.effect: AML 78.5% at UME vs 53.0% in AI-PAL; APL 2.4% vs 13.1%; lab distributions differed, most for monocytes.
links.quote: The proportion of acute leukaemia subtypes differed between the cohorts, with AML being more frequent at UME (78.5%) compared to the retrospective cohort of AI-PAL (53.0%), and APL being less common (2.4% vs 13.1%, respectively, Table 1 ).

links.outcome: Performance at new site versus original validation sites
links.effect: UME AUROC 0.67 for ALL and 0.71 for AML, below the worst prior validation site Créteil (0.78 and 0.80).
links.quote: This was a further degradation in model performance compared to the cohort from Créteil, which showed the worst model performance during validation, with an AUROC of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.67–0.89) for ALL and 0.80 (95% CI: 0.70–0.90) for AML.

links.outcome: Simulated real-world performance including differential diagnoses versus published results
links.effect: Adding differential diagnoses produced confident misclassifications as AML: 11.1% of MCL and 7.7% of MDS; performance lower than published results.
links.quote: The highest frequencies of ‘confident’ misclassification were observed for MCL and MDS, of which 11.1% (N = 2/18) and 7.7% (N = 3/39) were misclassified as AML, respectively ( Table 2 b).

links.outcome: Absence of safeguards for implausible or out-of-distribution inputs in AI-PAL
links.effect: Authors state no safeguards exist: predictions should be blocked for negative values or paediatric inputs, and a warning shown for OOD values.
links.quote: Last, a warning should be shown if the entered values are out-of-distribution (OOD).

links.outcome: Robustness of AI-PAL to missing laboratory values
links.effect: With 1-2 missing labs, AUROC by subtype was similar, while confident classifications decreased further.
links.quote: Overall, AUROC by AL subtypes were similar ( Supplementary Table S2b ), while confident classifications decreased further compared to patients with all laboratory values being available ( Supplementary Table S2c ).

links.outcome: Performance in an independent external local cohort versus developer-reported validation
links.effect: Independent validation at UME showed markedly lower AUROC (0.67 ALL, 0.71 AML) than published results.
links.quote: The AI-PAL algorithm demonstrated significantly lower performance in our simulated clinical implementation compared to prior published results.
